title: Ziklag Burned and Everything Recovered
summary: David and his men return from the Philistine muster to find Ziklag burned and their families carried off by Amalekite raiders. In grief his own men talk of stoning him, but David strengthens himself in the LORD, inquires through the priest Abiathar, and pursues. Guided by an abandoned Egyptian slave, he defeats the raiders and recovers everything, then decrees that those who stayed with the supplies share equally in the plunder and sends gifts to the elders of Judah.
story: While the Philistines and Israel prepare for battle at Gilboa, the story follows David south. He has been spared from fighting Israel (chapter 29), but he comes home to disaster. The Amalekite raid is a reversal of David's own raids in chapter 27: now his town is stripped, and his family is taken. It is the lowest point of his outlaw years, when even his loyal band turns against him. What happens next is the turning point. For the first time since he went over to the Philistines, David seeks the LORD, and from here on the story shows him acting like the king he is about to become. The chapter runs alongside Saul's last battle: while Saul, who failed to carry out the LORD's judgment on Amalek, is dying, David is defeating Amalek and beginning to govern.
historical:
The Amalekites were a seminomadic people of the southern deserts, remembered as Israel's first enemy after the exodus (Exodus 17). Saul's failure to deal with them in obedience to the LORD was the reason for his rejection (1 Samuel 15, repeated in 28:18). The raiders struck while the fighting men of the south were away with the armies, a classic tactic in desert warfare. They took captives rather than killing them, probably to sell as slaves, which is why the families could still be recovered.

The Brook of Besor is a seasonal streambed in the northwestern Negev, generally identified with the wadi now called Nahal Besor, which drains toward the coast near Gaza. The Cherethites, whose southern territory the Amalekites also raided, were a people associated with the Philistines and probably with Crete; men from this group later formed part of David's bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18). The towns listed at the end of the chapter (among them Aroer, Eshtemoa, Hormah, and Hebron) lie across the southern hill country and the Negev of Judah; the Bethel here is probably a southern town of that name rather than the famous Bethel north of Jerusalem.
cultural:
Stoning was the community's way of executing a person judged responsible for grave wrong, and the men's talk of stoning David shows how far their grief had turned into blame against their leader. David's response is the chapter's hinge: he “found strength in the LORD his God” and then calls for the ephod, the priestly garment with which the LORD's guidance was sought.

The treatment of the Egyptian slave reflects both the harshness and the hospitality of the desert. His master left him to die when he fell ill, a cheap calculation about a sick slave. David's men feed him first and question him afterward, and he asks for an oath that he will be neither killed nor handed back. The dispute over the plunder reflects the customs of war. Israel's law had already provided for dividing spoil between those who fought and the wider community (Numbers 31:27). David goes further, ruling that the men who guarded the baggage share equally with those who fought. The gifts he sends to the elders of Judah, described as a present from the plunder of the LORD's enemies, were a way of sharing victory with the towns that had sheltered him and of preparing their loyalty. The next chapter of the story begins with those same men of Judah anointing David at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:4).
literary: The chapter moves from total loss to total recovery, and the narrator underlines the reversal with repetition: the families were taken, and David recovered everything; “Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter” (verse 19). The structure follows a clear line: disaster (verses 1-6), inquiry (7-8), pursuit (9-15), victory (16-20), and a new law (21-25), closing with the list of gifts (26-31). Numbers carry the story: six hundred men set out, two hundred drop out exhausted, four hundred fight, and exactly four hundred Amalekites escape on camels. Two voices compete after the battle, the worthless men who want to exclude the weary and David who insists that the victory is the LORD's gift, not their achievement. The chapter closes on the name Hebron, where David will be crowned.

outline.t: Ziklag burned, and David's men turn against him
The pursuit and the Egyptian guide
The Amalekites defeated and everything recovered
Equal shares for those who stayed behind
Gifts to the elders of Judah

doctrines.note: In the worst moment of his life so far, with his family gone and his men against him, David strengthens himself in the LORD his God. Faith here is not a feeling but an act of turning toward God when every human support has collapsed.

David asks two plain questions through the ephod and receives a plain answer: pursue. After a long stretch in which David made decisions on his own, the chapter shows him seeking God before acting, and the difference is decisive.

David's ruling on the plunder is his first act of law-giving, and it rests on grace: “what the LORD has given us” cannot be hoarded by the strong. The kingdom God is building under David is meant to protect the weak and weary, not reward only the able.

words.note: Chazaq, to be strong, and in the form used in verse 6, to strengthen oneself or take courage. David's strength does not come from circumstances, which are ruinous, but from the LORD his God. The same verb appears in commands such as be strong and courageous (Joshua 1), and here it shows what such courage looks like from the inside.

Shalal, plunder or spoil. The word appears six times and becomes the center of the chapter's moral argument. The Amalekites feast on their plunder, David's men shout that it is David's plunder, the worthless men want to keep it from the weary, and David insists it is what the LORD has given. How the spoil is shared reveals the character of those who share it.

Beliyyaal, worthlessness, used in phrases for base or wicked people. It is the word for Eli's corrupt sons (2:12) and for Nabal (25:17). Later Jewish writings made Belial a name for an evil power, and Paul uses it that way in 2 Corinthians 6:15. Here it describes men whose greed would divide the community.

Choq, statute or decree, something fixed and binding. David's ruling becomes a statute and ordinance for Israel. The pairing with mishpat (ordinance) is common in the law of Moses, and the narrator presents David's decision as a lasting law of the kingdom, the act of a king before he wears the crown.

christ: The chapter prepares for David's kingship, and in doing so it shows traits the New Testament finds fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David. David goes after captives and brings every one of them back; Jesus describes himself as the shepherd who seeks the lost and loses none of those given to him (John 6:39, 10:28). David's ruling that the weary share the victory equally with the strong echoes the grace of the kingdom Jesus preached, in which the workers hired at the last hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day (Matthew 20:1-16). These are connections of pattern and character rather than predictions, but they show the kind of king Israel was learning to hope for.
questions: When everything collapsed, David strengthened himself in the LORD. What does that look like in practice for you when your usual supports give way?
The worthless men thought only those who fought deserved the reward. Where do you find it hard to share credit or blessing with those who could not keep up?
David's men fed the abandoned Egyptian before asking anything of him. Who are the overlooked people around you whose need you could meet first?
